transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what’s been bringing you here today?

Yeah… I guess the main thing is, I’m having a real problem at work now with heights—or not even heights in the abstract, but like, getting near scaffolding, roof edges, upper platforms, that kind of thing. I’m a construction manager, so it’s not like I can just avoid those areas all the time, and I know what the safety setup is supposed to look like. I can look right at the rails and see they’re in place, see that everything is supposed to be secure, and part of me knows it should be safe.

But as soon as I get near it, my head just goes, you’re going over. Like I’m about to tip or slip or somehow go right over the edge, even when there’s no real reason for that to happen. It’s gotten bad enough that I figured I needed to talk to somebody, because it’s not just a normal “be careful” feeling anymore.
Is this fear limited to being near heights or situations like scaffolding and roof edges, or do you find yourself feeling similarly anxious in other situations as well?

It’s really mostly that—being near the height itself, like the scaffolds, roof edges, upper platforms, that sort of thing. I mean, I’m here because every time I have to get close to one of those areas now, it’s like my brain immediately tells me, you’re about to go over. Even if I can literally see the guardrails are there, and I know the setup is supposed to be safe, it doesn’t seem to matter in the moment.

It’s not like I’m walking around anxious about everything all day, at least not in the same way. It’s when I get near those edges or elevated work areas that it really kicks in. Like my eyes can confirm one thing—rails in place, footing looks okay, the job site is set up right—but my body or my head is reacting like I’m already halfway over the side.

When you feel that fear near heights, do you find yourself actively avoiding those areas or situations if possible, like staying away from scaffolding or elevated platforms even when it’s part of your job?

Yes. Definitely. I’ve been avoiding them more than I want to admit, honestly.

Like, if there’s a height inspection that I technically should be doing myself, I’ve started handing those off to my foremen instead. I’ll tell myself it’s because they’re already closer to that part of the job or because I’m tied up with something else, but the truth is I’m arranging things so I don’t have to go up there if I can get out of it.

I’ve also been moving meetings down to ground level whenever I can. If we need to talk through something that’s happening on an upper platform or near a roof edge, I’ll try to have someone take pictures or describe it to me, or I’ll say we can discuss it from below. It’s embarrassing because I know, in my role, I’m supposed to be able to walk the site and check things directly.

And when I absolutely have to go up, I don’t like going alone anymore. I keep someone right beside me, almost like I need them there as an anchor or something. Then I rush through whatever I’m supposed to do. I’m not calmly inspecting it the way I used to—I’m just trying to get it over with while I’m scared the whole time.

When you’re near these heights or elevated areas and feel that fear, does your heart start racing, do you feel short of breath, or does anything else happen in your body that feels intense or overwhelming?

Yeah, it’s very physical. It’s not just a thought in my head.

The second I step onto those temporary stairs, or even just start walking toward an open upper floor, I can feel my chest tighten up. Like my whole upper body sort of clamps down before I’ve even gotten there. And my hands get wet—like actually sweaty—so then I’m aware of that too, which makes me feel even less steady.

The worst part is my legs. I get this feeling like they’re going to lock up on me, like I might not be able to make myself take the next step. I’ll be standing there trying to act normal because there are guys around me, and I’m supposed to be in charge, but inside I’m fighting with my own body just to keep moving. It feels really intense, like my body has decided there’s danger right now even if I’m telling myself the setup is safe.
